summary: Specifies how elliptic curve public keys are written in the Subject Public Key Information field of certificates. It describes the syntax and meaning of this field and updates parts of the earlier X.509 algorithm specification. This lets certificates carry keys for elliptic curve cryptography in a standard way.

eli5.summary: A certificate is like an ID card that holds someone's public key. This note says how to write a certain modern kind of key on that card, so every program reads it the same way.

questions: how are ecc keys encoded in x509 certificates
what is subject public key info for elliptic curves
what are compressed and uncompressed ec public keys
subtitle: How an elliptic curve public key is written into an X.509 certificate, and which curves and key uses are allowed.

tldr.problem: Certificates needed one agreed way to carry elliptic curve public keys, so that every program reads the same bytes the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The SubjectPublicKeyInfo field holds an algorithm identifier with named-curve parameters plus the key as an ECPoint, and the RFC says which key usage bits fit each identifier.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3279 and is itself updated by RFC 8813.

today: RFC 5480 is a Proposed Standard. It is updated by RFC 8813 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3279.

sections.title: What This RFC Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 5480 defines the format of the subjectPublicKeyInfo field in X.509 certificates that use Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). It covers keys for three families of algorithms: the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (ECMQV).

It updates RFC 3279, specifically Sections 2.3.5 and 5 and the ASN.1 module. Two ways of naming the allowed algorithms are defined: one lets the key be used with any ECC algorithm, the other restricts it to specific algorithms. The RFC says which one implementers must support, so that Certification Authorities and relying parties interoperate.
sections.eli5: Many programs need to put a special kind of lock key into a certificate. This note is the rulebook for how to write that key down so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Curve Parameters
sections.content:
A SubjectPublicKeyInfo is a sequence of an algorithm (an AlgorithmIdentifier) and the subjectPublicKey (a BIT STRING). Three algorithm identifiers are defined. id-ecPublicKey is unrestricted: the key is limited only by the key usage extension, it is also used with ECDSA, and it MUST be supported. id-ecDH and id-ecMQV restrict the key to that one key agreement algorithm, and both MAY be supported.

For all three, the parameters are ECParameters and MUST always be present. The only choice that may be used is namedCurve, an object identifier naming a well-known curve, and it MUST be supported. implicitCurve and specifiedCurve MUST NOT be used. If the curve parameters are missing, clients MUST reject the certificate.

The RFC publishes identifiers for the fifteen NIST-recommended curves, such as secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1. Other documents can publish identifiers for more curves.
sections.eli5: The card has a label saying what the key can do and which secret recipe it was made with. The recipe must always be named, never left blank.

sections.title: The Public Key Itself
sections.content:
The key is an ECPoint, which is an OCTET STRING, mapped bit for bit into the BIT STRING of subjectPublicKey. Implementations MUST support the uncompressed form and MAY support the compressed form. The hybrid form from X9.62 MUST NOT be used.

The first octet tells the form: 0x04 means uncompressed, and 0x02 or 0x03 means compressed. A public key with any other first octet MUST be rejected.
sections.eli5: The first byte of the key is a tiny sticker saying how the key was packed. If the sticker is not one of the allowed ones, you throw the key away.

sections.title: Key Usage Bits
sections.content:
The keyUsage extension says what a certificate's key may be used for. For a CA certificate with id-ecPublicKey, any combination of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyAgreement, keyCertSign and cRLSign MAY be present. The RFC recommends that if keyCertSign or cRLSign is present, then keyAgreement, encipherOnly and decipherOnly SHOULD NOT be present. For an end entity certificate, digitalSignature, nonRepudiation and keyAgreement MAY be present.

For id-ecDH or id-ecMQV, keyAgreement MUST be present, and either encipherOnly or decipherOnly MAY be. The values digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyTransport, keyCertSign and cRLSign MUST NOT be present.
sections.eli5: A key can be marked for signing papers or for agreeing on secrets. A key marked only for agreeing on secrets is not allowed to sign anything.

sections.title: Choosing Strengths and Curves
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3279 apply. A CA signing with ECDSA must pick a key size, a hash algorithm and a curve, and should make the bits of security of each roughly equivalent. The RFC gives a table of comparable minimums and a shorter RECOMMENDED table: secp192r1 with SHA-256 for 80 bits, secp224r1 with SHA-256 for 112 bits, secp256r1 with SHA-256 for 128 bits, secp384r1 with SHA-384 for 192 bits and secp521r1 with SHA-512 for 256 bits.

Using a larger hash and truncating it costs more processing than needed, which matters on constrained devices. The RFC also warns about keys that are not on well-known, widely reviewed curves, since they may be open to the MOV or Anomalous attacks, and says a candidate public key must be validated against its domain parameters. MD2 and MD5 are discouraged for new applications.
sections.eli5: A strong lock needs a strong door and a strong frame. The note says to pick key size, fingerprint method and curve that are all about equally strong, and to stick with curves that many experts have checked.

sections.title: ASN.1 Module and IANA
sections.content:
Appendix A holds an ASN.1 module that covers the ECC algorithms and also repeats the non-ECC ASN.1 from RFC 3279, so implementers need only this one module. It is a conformant subset of the X9.62 module. If an implementation needs the extra options in X9.62, it should use that module, particularly when it needs PER encoding, since output from the two modules might differ.

The RFC registers object identifiers for key types, curves and algorithms, mostly under the ANSI X9.62 arc, the hash algorithms in the NIST arc and many curves under the Certicom arc. It says no further action by IANA is necessary.
sections.eli5: The back of the note has the full list of exact word definitions, so program writers can copy one list instead of hunting through two.
